newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda adjourns first genocide trials in Kigali.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda adjourns first genocide trials in Kigali.

text.p: Two Rwandans appeared in court on Monday for the first genocide trials in the Rwandan capital but their cases were immediately adjourned.
Court officials said the trial of Silas Munyageshali, a former prosecutor in Kigali, was adjourned to an unnamed date in 1997 and was moved to the town of Gitarama south of Kigali.
The trial of Theodomir Ruzirabwoba, a former administrator in Kigali, was adjourned until January 3 to allow victims' counsel more time to compile evidence against him.
Faoduald Karamira, a prominent politician and former second vice-president of the Hutu MDR/Power party, did not appear in court as had been expected. No explanation was given.

Karamira is a former second vice-president of the Hutu extremist MDR/Power party. Karamira, from the town of Gitarama, was born an ethnic Tutsi but abandoned his roots and was identified and accepted as a Hutu.

He was a senior official of the extremist Interahamwe Hutu militia, accused of playing a leading role in the genocide in 1994 that killed up to one million people. Karamira was accused of speaking regularly on the Radio Mille Collines and Rwanda Radio, urging Hutus to slaughter rival Tutsi tribes people.
Deputy Justice Minister Gerard Gahima had earlier told reporters that Karamira, one of the most senior politicians in custody, would appear in court to face genocide charges.
"We don't know how many people we will be able to get through this week," Gahima said, and named Karamira and Munyageshali as two of those to be charged on Monday.

The first genocide trials in Rwanda opened on Friday in the southeastern town of Kibungo, where Deo Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former local administrator, both pleaded not guilty to organising massacres.
Gahima had also told reporters that between five or six people would be charged in Kigali and the government was contemplating possible public executions of those found guilty.
"If these men are found guilty and sentenced to death, we haven't decided whether executions will be public," Gahima added.
Those convicted on charges of taking part in the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis along with Hutu moderates face the death penalty after one chance of appeal.

In Tanzania on Sunday, officials declared an end to an operation to repatriate Rwandan refugees from Tanzania. Aid workers said nearly half a million Rwandan Hutus who fled to Tanzania after the genocide had returned home.
"The operation is winding down, overall it is finished," said Justin Cockerell, a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross in the northwestern Tanzanian town of Ngara.

"There no longer appear to be any large refugee groups," he told Reuters by telephone. "We see one or two sporadic family groups. We will be mopping up as clearly some people remain somewhere but it will be nothing like the same scale as before."
